_fields._note: Field documentation, not a case. The spec reads `cases` only. Convention change from the 20-case version: a case lists ONLY the fields it uses, instead of every field with nulls - at 46 rows the all-nulls form was unreadable. The spec must therefore validate required-fields-per-assert and throw naming the missing field, which is finding 2's lesson (guard the data file, it is the most volatile input) applied deliberately rather than by accident.
_fields.title: one-line intent; becomes the Playwright test title
_fields.channel: ui = assert on the /profile table | api = assert on an endpoint's response
_fields.account: which identity the browser logs in as: owner | empty | anonymous
_fields.acting_as: api channel only - whose token signs the request: owner | other | admin | none | ghost
_fields.session: valid | none | garbage | expired. Defaults to valid when omitted.
_fields.seed_owner_orders: orders to create for `owner` before asserting. Each entry is { status, total_amount? }. total_amount is sent to POST /api/checkout verbatim, including deliberately invalid values, because the endpoint takes it from the client with no server-side calculation. The backend only allows pending -> confirmed -> shipping -> delivered, so anything past pending costs several sequential admin calls; the fixture walks that chain.
_fields.seed_other_orders: how many orders to create under `other`, for the cross-tenant cases
_fields.transition_from: bring the seeded order to this status first, then attempt set_status
_fields.set_status: the status to attempt via PUT /api/admin/orders/:id/status, sent verbatim including out-of-set values
_fields.api_call: order_detail | admin_orders_list | admin_set_status | order_cancel | order_cancel_race | checkout | my_orders
_fields.detail_order_id: the raw id to put in the URL, as written - `abc`, `-1`, `0` are sent literally
_fields.detail_owned_by: whose order detail_order_id refers to: owner | other | nonexistent | seeded_first
_fields.cancel_target_status: the status the order must be in before the cancel attempt
_fields.expect_final_status: the status the order must hold after all concurrent actions finish
_fields.cancel_owned_by: whose order the cancel targets: owner | other
_fields.checkout_total_amount: the total_amount to send to POST /api/checkout, verbatim
_fields.act: a UI action the case performs before asserting: click_cancel
_fields.intercept: force an order-fetch response: my_orders_500 | my_orders_non_array | my_orders_nested_non_array
_fields.assert: UI rows only - which assertion block the spec runs. API rows do not carry it: they dispatch on `api_call`, because the endpoint IS the branch and a second name for the same thing could disagree with it. The spec validates each channel against the key that channel actually dispatches on, and both switches have an explicit default that throws on an unknown value.
_fields.expect_status: the seeded order status this row is about
_fields.expect_label: the Vietnamese label that status must render as (REQ-13)
_fields.expect_badge_class: the Tailwind classes carrying the colour requirement (REQ-14); the spec asserts both tokens are present, not that the class attribute equals this
_fields.expect_cancel_visible: whether the Hủy đơn button must be present for that status
_fields.expect_cancel_allowed: whether the cancel attempt must be permitted
_fields.expect_dialog: the text of the native alert the SUT uses as its only feedback channel (there is no toast, so getByRole('alert') matches nothing)
_fields.expect_label_after: the label the row must show after the attempted transition or action
_fields.expect_money_text: the exact rendered money cell, when it is assertable
_fields.expect_money_not: a substring the money cell must NOT contain
_fields.expect_row_count: exact number of rows expected. Null/omitted is the normal case: option A seeds per run and the SUT database is never reset, so the owner account accumulates orders and an absolute count would be wrong from run 2 onward. Rows are identified by the ids this run seeded instead.
_fields.expect_distinct_badge_count: how many mutually distinct badge colours must be on screen at once
_fields.expect_cancel_count: how many Hủy đơn buttons must be present among the seeded orders
_fields.expect_sorted_desc_by: column asserted to be newest-first. Only `order_id` is assertable: the rendered date column held exactly 1 distinct value across 16 orders because created_at is second-granularity and the cell uses toLocaleDateString(), which drops the time. The backend sorts ORDER BY id DESC.
_fields.expect_http_any_of: the acceptable HTTP statuses. A list, not a single value, where the requirement is 'must be refused' but the exact denial code is an unresolved open question (OQ-06, OQ-07, OQ-12, OQ-13). Asserting membership keeps the requirement testable without inventing a precision the design never had.
_fields.expect_http_multiset: the exact status multiset expected from concurrent requests; order does not matter
_fields.expect_total_amount: the independently chosen numeric amount whose API and rendered representations must agree
_fields.note: why this row exists, which HW02 gap or open question it closes, and - in prose only - whether it is expected to pass as a regression guard or to fail as a finding. Deliberately NOT a machine-readable field: nothing in the data file may give the spec a value it could use to soften or skip an assertion.

_identities._note: Changed from the approved matrix, which named ADMIN_EMAIL as the second identity for the ownership probe. Using the admin as the victim would confound 'a user read another user's order' with 'a user read an admin's data' - two different findings. `other` is now a fresh non-admin account per run, and the admin is used only for privileged setup.
_identities.owner: USER_EMAIL from .env - holds the orders under test
_identities.other: a fresh non-admin account the fixture registers per run - the cross-tenant victim
_identities.empty: a fresh non-admin account the fixture registers per run, never given an order
_identities.admin: ADMIN_EMAIL from .env - used only to walk status transitions during setup

cases.title: own orders are listed with all four fields, and another user's order is not
cases.note: HW02 TC-01, passed there. Patterns 1 + 3: the rendered rows must match the my-orders payload exactly, and the order seeded under `other` must appear in neither. Expected to pass - my-orders filters on user_id.

cases.title: a canceled order renders as Đã hủy with the red badge and no cancel button
cases.note: HW02 TC-02, passed there. Resolves OQ-05/OQ-08 for this status; label and colour read from Profile.jsx statusLabel/statusStyle and confirmed on the rendered page.

cases.title: a user with zero orders sees the empty state, not an error or a blank panel
cases.note: HW02 TC-08, passed there ([] at API level). Needs a fresh account: USER_EMAIL and ADMIN_EMAIL both hold orders now, so neither can serve this case. The spec must wait for the my-orders response first - `orders` initialises to [] so the empty-state text renders before the fetch resolves, which would make this pass for a user who does have orders. See TC-36 for the defect this shares a rendering path with.

cases.title: a pending order renders as Chờ xác nhận with the yellow badge and a cancel button
cases.note: Derived addition. Closes HW02 EC-09, recorded there as 'may be incidentally observed but cannot be asserted as guaranteed or deliberate' - seeding the status makes it deliberate. Note yellow is statusStyle's default branch, so an unknown status would also render yellow; TC-13 and TC-25 are what distinguish them.

cases.title: a confirmed order renders as Đã xác nhận with the indigo badge and a cancel button
cases.note: Derived addition. Closes HW02 EC-10, 'Not covered - setup dependency' (OQ-15); reachable via PUT /api/admin/orders/:id/status, verified working.

cases.title: a shipping order renders as Đang giao with the blue badge
cases.note: Derived addition, closes HW02 EC-11. **Deliberately asserts label and colour only** - it is the one status_badge row that omits expect_cancel_visible. Earlier it carried `true`, which locked in what this build renders: a SUT fixed by hiding the button on shipping would have turned this positive case red. The cancel requirement for shipping is owned by TC-14 (count) and TC-26/TC-27 (enforcement), so the defect produces one red owner per layer instead of also corrupting the status-rendering oracle.

cases.title: a delivered order renders as Đã giao with the green badge and no cancel button
cases.note: Derived addition, closes HW02 EC-12. Reaching delivered costs three sequential admin calls (pending -> confirmed -> shipping -> delivered); the state machine permits no shortcut, which TC-24 verifies.

cases.title: all five statuses on screen at once are mutually distinct in colour
cases.note: Derived addition. REQ-14 requires colours to distinguish statuses, and HW02 only ever observed one status at a time, so an 'all badges identical' defect was structurally invisible to it. DIAGNOSTIC for the TC-02/09/10/11/12 cluster: if all five go red together, this one row says whether the cause is one shared styling fault or five separate label faults.

cases.title: cancel is offered only on the two statuses a customer may still cancel
cases.note: Derived addition. UI-only behaviour (Profile.jsx L200) with no API equivalent, so HW02 could not see it at all. **Oracle taken from the requirement, not from the build.** The count is 2 - pending and confirmed - because that is the rule the implementation itself names: `server.js:344` carries `// Lẽ ra phải là: if (order.status !== 'pending' && order.status !== 'confirmed')`, so the documented intent is that a shipping order is no longer customer-cancellable. The build renders 3 (probe: 14 buttons across 16 orders, absent only on delivered and canceled), so this row is **expected to fail**, and it fails for the same cause as TC-26/TC-27. An earlier version of this row said 3, which would have locked the defect in as the expected result and turned a correct fix red. Counted across the five seeded rows rather than the whole table, because the owner account accumulates orders across runs.

cases.title: the list is deterministically newest-first
cases.note: Derived addition, closes FR §7 'list sort order and deterministic tie-breaking', never resolved and never tested. Asserted on the Mã ĐH column, NOT on the date: 16 orders produced exactly 1 distinct rendered date, so the date column cannot witness ordering. The backend's ORDER BY id DESC is what makes ties deterministic - three orders seeded in the same second are the tie.

cases.title: the order date renders as a real date, not Invalid Date or blank
cases.note: Derived addition, closes FR §7 'order date format', never resolved. Profile.jsx L186 does new Date(o.created_at).toLocaleDateString() on a SQLite 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS' string; that form is non-standard for Date.parse, so it is accepted by engine convention rather than by spec. The case most likely to differ across the three engines, which is why it is worth running on all three. The assertion must not hardcode a locale string - the rendered format is the engine's, not the app's.

cases.title: with no session, the order history is not shown
cases.note: HW02 TC-04, 401 at API level. At the UI there is no redirect: /profile stays at /profile and renders 'Vui lòng đăng nhập' with no table at all. Asserting the table is absent as well as the message, so that a future build which renders an empty table cannot pass on the message alone.

cases.title: a garbage token is rejected and no order history is shown
cases.note: HW02 TC-05, 403 at API level; confirms OQ-07 at the UI layer. There is no UI path that produces a bad token, so it is injected into localStorage['token'] - the key AuthContext reads. AuthContext calls logout() when /api/users/me rejects it, so the expected end state is the same as TC-04; the point of keeping both is that they arrive there by different routes.

cases.title: one user must not be able to read another user's order by ID
cases.note: HW02 TC-03, FAILED there: HTTP 200, no ownership check (BUG-07). server.js:360 confirms GET /api/orders/:id carries no authenticateToken at all. Expected to fail here too - per project rule §4 that is a finding, not an assertion to soften. The denial code is left as a set because OQ-06 (denial shape) is moot while no check exists. TC-28 is the control that proves the codebase CAN check ownership, which sharpens this into 'the detail route forgot' rather than 'the app has no concept of ownership'.

cases.title: the order-detail route must also refuse a request with no token
cases.note: Derived addition. Closes the explicit scope trade-off HW02 recorded in 03 §2: 'REQ-02's auth enforcement is not independently re-verified... a symmetric pair of TCs could be added later if full per-endpoint auth coverage is wanted'. Expected to fail, same root cause as TC-03: the route has no auth middleware. Kept separate because authentication and authorisation are different requirements and a fix for one need not fix the other.

cases.title: a nonexistent order ID is reported as not found
cases.note: HW02 TC-06, passed there (404). The one unambiguous expectation among the id probes, which makes it the baseline the four ⚠️ rows below are read against.

cases.title: a malformed order ID must not return an order
cases.note: HW02 TC-07, saw 404 - indistinguishable from a nonexistent id, which is what OQ-12/OQ-13 asks about. 400 would be the more precise answer for a non-numeric id; 404 is defensible. The requirement not in question is 'must not serve an order', so that is what is asserted. Recorded as an open question in the report rather than settled by the test.

cases.title: order ID -1, below the lower boundary
cases.note: HW02 BVA-01, saw 404. OQ-17 asks whether any distinct sign or range check exists; the 404 suggests not, i.e. it falls through to 'no such row'. Asserted as 'rejected or not found' so the case stays honest about which of the two it cannot distinguish.

cases.title: order ID 0, immediately below the first valid ID
cases.note: HW02 BVA-02, saw 404. Paired with BVA-03 this is the real boundary: 0 must miss and 1 must hit. AUTOINCREMENT starts at 1, so 0 can never name a row.

cases.title: order ID 1, the first valid ID, is served
cases.note: HW02 BVA-03, saw 200 - ids are 1-indexed, which resolves OQ-16. Depends on order id 1 existing: orders.id is AUTOINCREMENT from 1 and database.js recreates the table on every backend start, so id 1 exists as soon as anything has been seeded - hence the seed on this row. If the backend is restarted mid-suite this is the row that will notice first.

cases.title: a non-admin user must not be able to list every order in the system
cases.note: NEW. GET /api/admin/orders (server.js:526) carries authenticateToken but no role check, so any logged-in user can read every order in the database - the same requirement TC-03 tests, breached through a different door and at far greater scale (all orders at once, with users.name joined in). Expected to fail with 200. Shares a root cause with TC-19.

cases.title: a non-admin user must not be able to change an order's status
cases.note: NEW. PUT /api/admin/orders/:id/status (server.js:541) carries authenticateToken but no role check, so a plain user can drive the order lifecycle. This is not merely an admin-feature bug: the status column is what FR-11 exists to display, so a user-writable status means the history can be made to show anything. Expected to fail with 200. Shares a root cause with TC-18 - if both go red, the finding is 'no admin endpoint checks role', not two separate holes.

cases.title: a canceled order must not be transitionable to delivered
cases.note: NEW, and the highest-value case in this file. server.js:566 contains an explicit `if (currentStatus === 'canceled' && status === 'delivered') isValidTransition = true;` - a canceled order can be resurrected as delivered. Every other backwards or skipping transition is refused, so this is a specific hole rather than a missing check, which TC-24 proves. Expected to fail with 200. TC-23 is the same defect witnessed at the UI, where it does its actual damage.

cases.title: an order the user canceled must never display as Đã giao
cases.note: NEW. The UI consequence of TC-22, and the form the defect takes for the customer: an order they cancelled appears in their own history as delivered, with a green badge, and with the cancel button gone. Kept separate from TC-22 because FR-11 is a display requirement - the API contract breach and the false display are two different findings with two different severities, and this is the one a user would report.

cases.title: a status transition that skips the chain is refused
cases.note: NEW. CONTROL for TC-22. pending -> delivered is not in the transition table, so this must be refused. Expected to pass. Its value is entirely in what it proves about TC-22: if this refuses and TC-22 permits, the finding is 'one specific illegal transition was whitelisted', which is a far more precise and more damning bug report than 'transition validation is broken'.

cases.title: an out-of-set status value is refused, so it can never reach the badge renderer
cases.note: NEW. Converts HW02 EC-14 from 'deliberately not automated' into a reachability probe. EC-14 was excluded on the grounds that no valid request makes a correct system produce an anomalous status - this row tests that premise instead of assuming it. If it returns 200, statusLabel falls back to status.toUpperCase() and the history renders a raw 'HACKED' badge in default yellow, i.e. indistinguishable from Chờ xác nhận. Expected to pass (isValidTransition stays false), and worth having precisely because a pass is what justifies EC-14's exclusion.

cases.title: cancel must be refused on an order that is already shipping
cases.note: NEW. server.js:344 guards cancel with `status === 'delivered' || status === 'canceled'`, and the line above it carries the developer's own comment: `// Lẽ ra phải là: if (order.status !== 'pending' && order.status !== 'confirmed')`. So an order already in transit can be cancelled by the customer, and Profile.jsx offers the button for it. Expected to fail. This is the row that asserts the requirement, against TC-11 which asserts the build - the pair is deliberate, not contradictory.

cases.title: the cancel endpoint itself must refuse a shipping order
cases.note: NEW. Same defect as TC-26 at the API layer. Kept because it answers the triage question TC-26 alone cannot: whether the fix belongs in the button's visibility condition or in the endpoint's guard. If the UI hid the button but the endpoint still accepted the request, the vulnerability would remain while looking fixed.

cases.title: a user must not be able to cancel another user's order
cases.note: NEW. CONTROL for TC-03 and TC-15. The cancel handler scopes its lookup with `WHERE id = ? AND user_id = ?` (server.js:339), so this must be refused. Expected to pass - and that pass is what makes TC-03's failure a specific omission on the detail route rather than a system with no concept of ownership. The two rows together are a much stronger bug report than either alone. `cancel_target_status` is `pending` so the integrity check actually runs: a 404 that cancelled the order anyway would otherwise pass on the status code alone. The check must read through `other`'s own token - my-orders filters on user_id, so asking with the owner's token would return nothing and pass on `undefined`.

cases.title: cancelling an already-canceled order is refused
cases.note: NEW. The guard explicitly covers this branch, so expected to pass. Included as the second half of the guard's coverage: TC-26/27 probe what it wrongly allows, this and TC-30 confirm what it correctly blocks, which is what tells a fixer that the condition needs widening rather than rewriting.

cases.title: cancelling a delivered order is refused
cases.note: NEW. Expected to pass; pairs with TC-29. Also the counterpart to TC-12's expect_cancel_visible: false - together they check that a delivered order is protected at both the UI and the endpoint, which is the standard TC-26 shows shipping fails to meet.

cases.title: a non-numeric order total must not render as NaN
cases.note: NEW. POST /api/checkout writes total_amount straight from the request body with no validation or server-side recalculation (server.js:313), and SQLite is dynamically typed so a string lands in the INTEGER column intact. Profile.jsx L189 then does Number(o.total_amount || 0).toLocaleString(), which yields the literal string 'NaN' - so the history displays 'NaN ₫' as a price. Reachable by any authenticated client. Expected to fail. TC-35 is the diagnostic for the shared cause.

cases.title: an order total of zero renders as a zero amount
cases.note: NEW. Lower boundary of the money column. Expected to pass as a display, while noting that a zero-total order being accepted at all is a checkout-side question outside FR-11's boundary. Paired with TC-34 to ask whether 'zero' and 'missing' are distinguishable to the customer - they are not, both render 0 ₫.

cases.title: a negative order total must not be displayed as a price
cases.note: NEW. Same reachability as TC-31: the client supplies total_amount. The cell renders '-1,000,000 ₫' in the red bold styling used for prices. Expected to fail. The boundary is stated honestly in the report: the missing input validation is checkout's, but a customer-facing history that presents a negative number as an amount owed is FR-11's display requirement, and the two findings should be filed against their own components.

cases.title: a missing order total must not be silently displayed as 0 ₫
cases.note: NEW. Profile.jsx's `o.total_amount || 0` fallback turns absent data into a confident-looking 0 ₫, so a data-integrity failure is presented to the customer as a real price of zero rather than as unavailable. Expected to fail against that requirement. Distinct from TC-32 in input and in meaning even though both render the same string - which is precisely the finding.

cases.title: checkout must reject a non-numeric order total
cases.note: NEW. DIAGNOSTIC for TC-31, TC-33 and TC-34. All three are display symptoms of one cause: checkout trusts a client-supplied total. This row isolates that cause in a single assertion, so a wall of red in the money column resolves to one root finding instead of three. Expected to fail with 200. Deliberately kept as one row rather than three parallel checkout probes - negative, zero and non-numeric all fail for the same missing validation.

cases.title: a failed order fetch must be reported as an error, not as an empty history
cases.note: NEW, and the strongest UI-side finding available. Profile.jsx's fetchOrders catch block does setOrders([]), so a server error, a network failure and a genuinely empty account all render the identical 'Bạn chưa có đơn hàng nào.'. A customer whose orders failed to load is told they have never ordered anything. Forced with route interception returning 500, which is legitimate: the requirement is about how the page handles a failure, and no other input can produce one on demand. Expected to fail. Note this makes TC-08 weaker than it looks - it passes for the right reason only because the fetch succeeds.

cases.title: an unexpected response shape must not break the page
cases.note: NEW. Profile.jsx guards with `Array.isArray(res.data) ? res.data : res.data.orders || []`, so this branch exists and is worth exercising. Expected to pass - included because the guard's presence shows the author anticipated a shape change, which makes it a real contract the page relies on rather than an invented risk.

cases.title: a successful cancel confirms the outcome to the user
cases.note: NEW. The happy path of the Thao tác column, never exercised by HW02, which only ever read the list. Also records a fact the automation has to live with: the SUT's only feedback channel here is a native alert (Profile.jsx cancelOrder), so BasePage.toast / getByRole('alert') matches nothing and the assertion has to capture the dialog. Expected to pass.

cases.title: the list reflects the new status without a manual reload
cases.note: NEW. cancelOrder calls fetchOrders() after a success, so the row should update in place; expected to pass. Distinct requirement from TC-38 - one is 'the user is told', the other is 'the screen stops lying' - and a stale-list defect is the kind that survives a passing dialog assertion. Seeded as confirmed rather than pending so this is not a duplicate transition of TC-38.

cases.title: one rendered row matches the API payload across ID, date, total and status
cases.note: Coverage correction. TC-01's title says all four fields, but its assertion compared only the set of order IDs. This case gives each displayed field an owner: exact ID, a non-empty real date, independently supplied total and the status label. Expected to pass; it detects column swaps or a row assembled from values belonging to different orders.

cases.title: an expired but correctly signed token is rejected before history loads
cases.note: A garbage JWT and an expired valid-signature JWT reach different jwt.verify branches. This control makes sure TC-05 is not only proving syntax rejection. Expected to pass with /api/users/me = 403 and no order table.

cases.title: a nested orders value of the wrong type must not crash the profile
cases.note: TC-37 covers the intended {orders:[...]} fallback only. Profile.jsx trusts res.data.orders without checking that the nested value is an array; a truthy string reaches orders.map and can crash React. Expected to fail, isolating response-shape validation from TC-36's HTTP-error handling.

cases.title: a validly signed token for a deleted or nonexistent user is not a live session
cases.note: authenticateToken verifies only the signature and never establishes that req.user.id still exists. A ghost identity must not receive even an empty order-history payload. Expected to fail with 200 []; distinct from malformed/expired-token rejection because the signature is valid.

cases.title: the cancel endpoint refuses a request with no token and preserves the order
cases.note: Auth control for the mutation endpoint. TC-15 proves the detail route forgot auth; this row verifies the cancel route does not share that omission and that denial leaves state untouched. Expected to pass.

cases.title: two simultaneous cancel requests acknowledge the transition only once
cases.note: Concurrency probe. Both requests may read pending before either UPDATE completes, causing two 200 responses for one state transition. The required outcome is one success, one refusal, final status canceled. Expected to expose a check-then-update race while remaining deterministic about the final state.
